EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


      Interest in the use of a copper nickel alloy for OTEC applications has cen­
tered on the alloy designated as C70600 containing nominally 10% nickel with  an
appropriate amount of iron.  This alloy has the advantage of a lower cost and
 superior resistance to biofouling as compared with alloys of higher nickel
content.  Data for the C71500 alloy and other copper base alloys are included in
 this review for convenient comparison.   Some data on the C71900 and C72200
alloys are also included.  These alloys vrould be appropriate where increased
 resistance to erosion would be needed.


     Thouqh the resistance of the C70600 alloy to corrosion by seawater can be
expected to provide the desired 30 year life for evaporators or condensers,
 inadeauate resistance to corrosion by ammonia removes this alloy as a candidate
so long as ammonia is to be the working fluid in closed cvcle systems,   ^lie
conclusion  is reinforced by the existence of peculations of the U.S. Coast Guard
 (CG257)  and the Interqovenmental Maritime Consultative Orqanization  (IMCO)
 (section 154.1700, Table 4).  These peculations prohibit the use of copper
alloys in contact with ammonia.

      However,  in view of the possibility of usinc freon or some other non-
corrosive workinc fluid, continuinq attention to copper-nickel alloys is
warranted.  This extends to heat exchanqers  in open cycle systems as well as to
other components that would not be in contact with ammonia and where resistance
to macrofoulinq is desired.

     Another means of dealinq with the problem of corrosion by ammonia would be
throuqh the use of a duplex or triplex metal combination with steel on the
ammonia side and the C70600 alloy on the seawater side.

     A triplex combination using  a 30% nickel C71500 alloy clad with the C70600
alloy for the seawater side may be preferred.  The C70600 alloy would be anodic
to the C71500 alloy and  vrould be analaqous to Alclad.   The favorable galvanic
effect would arrest penetration of the more noble C71500 alloy by tolerable sac­
rificial corrosion of the C70600 alloy cladding.  The advantage of the proposed
combination would extend to thin wall tubes or plates  in heat exchanqers even  if
ammonia were not to be used as the working fluid.

      It will be necessary to identify appropriate antifouling countermeasures to
maintain heat transfer efficiency without intolerable acceleration of corrosion
by either mechanical cleaning  (e.q., Amertap”) or chlorination or some combina­
tion of these.  Mechanical cleaning presents more of a hazard than chlorination.
It  is likely that compatible means for periodic in-place chemical cleaning of
plate type heat exchanqers can be devised.


     There  is a remaining need to establish the ability of a copper nickel allov
to resist the erosive effects of turbulence that miqht be created by particular
configurations of the surfaces of plates  in plate-tvpe heat exchangers.

     The resistance of C70600 alloy to macro-biofoulinq makes it attractive for
use in such components as screens, piping, water boxes and tube plates.  Use  in
the latter application would be restricted to heat exchangers with copper nickel
tubes.  The C70600 alloy is sufficiently anodic to stainless steels or titanium
to remove it from consideration for tube plates in conjunction with these tube
materials.



                                         ix

Use of the C70600 alloy in piping and water boxes would not be proper  in
conjunction with downstream aluminum because of an intolerable effect on corro­
sion of aluminum by copper released by corrosion of C70600 alloy.  This restric­
tion need not extend to the use of the alloy for screens in view of the small
area of the copper alloy,  the low rate of release of copper ions and the large
mass of water.   The amount of copper that might be released by a copper nickel
screen is not likely to exceed 0.01 part per billion depending on the area of
the screen and the volume of water  flow.

      The matter of release of copper  ions from C70600 alloy components will have
to be taken into account in connection with any limits on such release that mav
be imposed by FPA regulations.   It should be possible to establish that the
extent of any release of copper ions as related to the "baseline" concentration
of copper  in water at potential OTEC locations can be tolerated ecoloqically.

     The copper nickel alloys are amenable to fabrication by all common methods.
Thev have adequate mechanical properties and are covered bv applicable construc­
tion codes.  The C7nfi00 alloy is available in all the forms and in the quanti­
ties required for proposed OTEC applications.   It compares advantaaeouslv with
other candidate materials  (such as titanium and stainless steels of high chro­
mium and molybdenum content)  with respect to existing production capacity for
the possibly larqe quantities of the metals that should be needed.   This extends
to the size of the base of any larqe scale expansion of production that miqht be
required to accomodate the high levels of OTEC power capacity projected in some
recent targets.

FOREWORD




      The suitability of copper nickel alloys for use for components of Ocean
Thermal Energy Conversion  (OTEC)  Systems has been examined by scrutiny of data
from appropriate tests and records in related applications.   This review is
based on two surveys of pertinent data.  The first was carried out  for the U.S.
Department of Energy by J. A. Beavers and W.  K. Boyd of Battelle Columbus
Laboratories.  The second was an extension of the Battelle report by  R.  0.  Lewis
of the LaQue Center for Corrosion Technology,  Inc. under contract with Argonne
National Laboratories, again, on behalf of the U.S. Department of Energy.   The
present exercise presents a condensation of the R.  0. Lewis report which incor­
porated data from the Battelle report.

INTRODUCTION



      The feasibility of Ocean Thermal Enerqy Conversion  (OTEC) power qeneration
is presently receivinq a comprehensive evaluation by the U.S. Department of
Enerqy.  Operatinq as a "closed" loop Rankine thermodynamic cycle, an OTEC
system, now beinq considered, utilizes ammonia as a workinq fluid.  The fluid  is
expanded and condensed by warm ocean surface waters and deep, cold waters,
respectively.  Because of the relatively small temperature difference and driv-
inq force available, thermal efficiency of the condensers and evaporators  is
critical to the economic viability of an OTEC system.

      The tarqet for heat exchanqer tubinq materials for OTEC condensers and
evaporators includes the followinq performance criteria to be acceptable:

       1.  Marine corrosion resistance to afford  a proiected 30 vear life.

       2.   Inherent antifoulinq properties and/or resistance to chemical/
         mechanical cleaninq methods.

      3.  Corrosion resistance to ammonia and ammonia plus seawater mixtures.

       4.  Adequate mechanical properties.

       5.  Availability in the required forms.

       6.  Amenability to conventional fabrication practices.

     The several materials beinq considered  for OTEC heat exchanqer tubinq in­
clude copper-nickel alloys and particularly C70600,  a 90-10 copper-nickel alloy
containing iron.  A well documented history of usaqe aboard naval vessels and  in
coastal power plant condensers and desalination plants supports the qualifica­
tion of 90-10 and other copper-nickel alloys  for use  in OTEC heat exchanqers.   A
major impediment to their use is imposed by susceptibility to corrosion by
ammonia and ammonia plus seawater.   The followinq survey summarizes pertinent
information on the use and application of copper-nickel alloys in marine
environments.

      The qualification of copper-nickel alloy tubinq for OTEC heat exchanqers is

                         SEAWATER CORROSION RESISTANCE

     Copper-nickel alloys of commercial interest to OTEC as heat exchanqer
tubinq materials, C70600  (90/10), C71500  (70/30)  and C72200  (R4/16, 0.5%Cr),
have been shown, both in the laboratory and in service, to possess excellent
corrosion resistance  in seawater. Fiqure  3,  from Tuthill and Schillmoller,24
shows averaqe corrosion rates for both C70600 and C71500 in the ranqe of
2.5 microns per year,  pm/y,  (0.1 mils per year, mpy)  to 12.7 pm/y (0.5 mpy)  .
Southwell et  al.2f1 and Efird and Anderson8^ performed lonq term evalua­
tions and results of the latter are shown in Fiqures  4 and  5.   After 14-16 vears
exposure to quiescent and low velocity seawater, both materials exhibited corro­
sion rates less than 2.5 pm/yr  (0.1 mpy).


     These lonq term corrosion rates are important  in accurately assessing the
projected life of a condenser.  Because of the parabolic nature of copper nickel
weight loss in seawater over extended time periods,  an inaccurate estimate of
life can be projected from short term tests.   Wieiqht loss measurements after one
to two years exposure can lead to predictions of lonq term corrosion rates up to
five times the actual measured rates.

     Both alloys C70600 and C71500 display excellent resistance to pitting  in
seawater.  The averaqe depth of the twenty deepest pits in C71500 observed by
Southwell88 was less than  127 pm  (5 mils)  after  16 years exposure.  Tuthill
and Schillmoller24 reviewed the pitting resistance of materials  in quiescent

seawater and concluded that,  for both C70600 and C71500, penetration rates are
conservatively less than  127 pm/y  (5 mpy),  as shown  in Fiqure  6.

     Chromium modified Cu-Ni alloys, developed for resistance to hiqh velocity
seawater, have been evaluated  in both low and hiqh velocity conditions.

     Maximum resistance to high velocity seawater by a Cu-Ni alloy has been

     The overall performance of copper base alloys  in seawater  is attributed  to
the growth of a corrosion product film which in the classical sense  is
"passive".  This film growth may require very long times to reach steady state
as shown by Efird31  in Figures  4 and  5.   In quiet seawater, this time span
approaches four years while,  in flowing seawater, the corrosion rate continually
decreases over at least a  14 year period.

      In seawater, the corrosion product  is predominately CU2O  (cuprous oxide)
irrespective of alloy composition.36'3^  Often observed  in addition to the
red-brown CU2O is the compound Paratacamite  (CU2(OH)3CI),  a bulky, green,
non-protective corrosion product overlaying the CU2O.

      The morphology, composition and growth kinetics of the passive film on
Cu-Ni alloys have been studied by North and Pryor,36 Popplewell et al.,37
Kievits and Ijsseling,36 and Blundy and Pryor.39

            The anodic reaction 2Cu + H2O —> CU2O + 2H+ +  2e


                                         and

             the cathodic reaction O2 + 2H2O + 4e— —> 40H-,

describe the generally accepted reactions that occur as copper corrodes  in aer­
ated seawater.   As the CU2O corrosion product film qrows, copper  ions and
electrons must pass through the film to support the anodic and cathodic half
reactions. Experimental results obtained by North and Pryor36 and supported
by others37-39 show that alloying additions of nickel and  iron to copper
improves corrosion resistance.  The mechanism is proposed as the incorporation
of Ni2+ and Fe3+ ions into the highly defective, p-tvpe Cu20 corrosion
product film as "dopants" altering the defect structure.

     Parrish^O demonstrated electrochemically that the rate of passive film
formation is greater on the iron containing 90/10 Cu-Ni alloy than on the iron
free composition, and that the passive film on 90/10 with iron  is more protec­
tive as indicated by lower passive current density.

As shown  in Tables V and VI by North and Pryor,siqnificant36              increases
in electronic and ionic resistivity of CujO occur with the addition of nickel
and iron.  The resistivity results indicate that Ni2+ occupies cation vacan­
cies and substitutional sites equally in the corrosion product on the 90/10
Cu-Ni alloy.  The additional nickel available  in the 70/30 Cu-Ni alloy increases
electronic resistivity quite measurably but ionic resistivity only sliqhtly.
This suqqests incorporation of Ni2+  in 70/30 oxide films  is mostly by sub­
stitution for Cu+.   Iron additions to 90/10 and 70/30 result  in incorporation
of Fe2+ by substitution,  thereby,  further increasinq electronic resistivity.
The corrosion rate of Cu-Ni alloys is largely controlled by the resistance
characteristics of the CuoO film and the rate has been shown by North and
Pryor,in Fiqure 9, to be inversely proportional to the sum of the elec­
tronic and ionic resistances of compact CU2O films.

     Palmer and Wilson^ attempted to show,  throuqh microstructural analy­
sis, that sinqle phase equilibria defined the upper limits for useful iron

diagram for a sinqle phase structure.

and corrosion product composition for several Cu-Ni alloys in quiet and flowinq
